# Abstract

**Background:** Health financing research in Kenya, including studies based on the Demographic and Health Survey (DHS), routinely defines its study population by *self-reported diagnosis*: people reporting that a health worker told them they have hypertension or diabetes. Treatment gaps, financial protection and insurance coverage are then estimated within that diagnosed subpopulation. If self-report captures only a minority of those living with disease, such estimates describe a privileged subset of the population in need and leave the unreached majority invisible. We quantify this denominator problem for Kenya and its sex disparities.

**Methods:** We compared measured disease prevalence from Kenya STEPS 2015, which measured blood pressure and fasting glucose, with self-reported diagnosis prevalence from KDHS 2022, which records self-report only. The KDHS chronic-disease module was administered only to women in Long Questionnaire households, so we applied stratum-specific reweighting to preserve national representativeness before pooling with male subsample-reweighted men. The detection ratio is self-reported prevalence divided by measured prevalence; the underdiagnosis index is one minus that ratio. Because KDHS caps women at 49 and men at 54 while STEPS covers ages 18 to 69, the age-comparable 18–49 window is primary and full-survey estimates secondary. Confidence intervals come from 2,000 stratified primary sampling unit bootstrap replications, the two surveys resampled independently. Awareness is reported under both "ever told" and "told within 12 months" definitions to reconcile with the published national cascade.

**Results:** Among adults aged 18–49, measured hypertension prevalence was 19.8% (95% CI 17.5% to 22.5%) against self-reported diagnosis of 6.6% (6.2% to 7.1%), a detection ratio of 0.334 (0.288 to 0.383): two in three adults with hypertension are absent from self-report denominators. Detection diverged sharply by sex. Women had measured prevalence of 17.5% (15.2% to 20.1%) and self-reported diagnosis of 9.5% (8.8% to 10.3%), a ratio of 0.542 (0.459 to 0.638). Men had the higher measured prevalence, 22.2% (19.0% to 25.8%), but the lower self-report, 3.3% (2.9% to 3.8%), giving a ratio of 0.151 (0.123 to 0.185) and an underdiagnosis index of 84.9% (81.5% to 87.7%). Across full survey age ranges the pooled ratio was 0.281 (0.250 to 0.315). At population level, 16.2% (14.3% to 18.4%) of adults aged 18–49 had unaware hypertension and 19.4% (17.0% to 22.1%) uncontrolled hypertension. Among diagnosed adults, 32.1% (29.0% to 35.2%) were on medication and 45.6% (42.3% to 48.8%) insured; scaled to the population, treatment reached 2.1% (1.9% to 2.4%) of adults. For diabetes the ratio was 0.754 (0.536 to 1.116), from only 60 measured cases.

**Conclusions:** Self-reported diagnosis captures only one in three Kenyan adults with hypertension, and less than one in six men. Health financing metrics and treatment gaps conditioned on self-report do not represent the population in need; they describe a selected minority who have successfully navigated primary care detection hurdles. As Kenya implements the Social Health Authority, financing monitoring reliant on self-report will record progress among the already-diagnosed while the undiagnosed majority remains uncounted. Routine measured surveillance is an essential precondition for interpreting household health financing evidence.

**Keywords:** hypertension; diabetes; underdiagnosis; self-reported diagnosis; health financing; measurement; Demographic and Health Survey; STEPS; Kenya; Social Health Authority

# Background

Kenya's transition from the National Hospital Insurance Fund (NHIF) to the Social Health Authority (SHA) on 1 October 2024 has heightened the demand for empirical evidence regarding population coverage, treatment gaps, and financial risk protection [@nungo2024; @barasa2018]. Much of the national evidence base for non-communicable diseases (NCDs) relies on large-scale household surveys, specifically the Demographic and Health Survey (DHS). In the 2022 Kenya Demographic and Health Survey (KDHS), NCD assessment rests upon a self-report screening module: whether respondents report having been informed by a doctor, nurse, or other health professional that they have high blood pressure or diabetes [@kdhs2022]. Secondary analyses of these data have produced important insights into insurance disparities, catastrophic expenditures, and treatment shortfalls among adults living with diagnosed disease [@amollo2026st03].

However, this analytical framework carries a critical methodological limitation that is frequently acknowledged in passing but rarely quantified. An individual can only report a diagnosis if two prior events have occurred: they must have had contact with a healthcare provider, and that provider must have performed a diagnostic test and communicated the finding. Consequently, self-reported diagnosis reflects the joint probability of *having biological disease* and *having been successfully identified by the health system*. Where screening coverage is low or episodic, the diagnosed population represents a highly selected subpopulation that may differ fundamentally in demographic composition, socioeconomic status, healthcare utilisation, and financial vulnerability from the broader population living with undiagnosed disease [@vellakkal2013; @singh2022].

For health financing and universal health coverage (UHC) monitoring, this denominator distortion has serious policy implications. When studies report that 68% of diagnosed hypertensive adults in Kenya are not taking prescribed medication, this treatment gap is conditioned entirely on individuals who have already cleared the detection hurdle [@amollo2026st03]. It remains silent on the population with active disease who never entered the denominator. If the majority of individuals with disease are undiagnosed, then universal health coverage indicators that evaluate financial protection only among the diagnosed track performance within a small, relatively privileged fraction of need.

Quantifying the extent of this underdiagnosis gap requires benchmarking self-reported survey data against objective, biomarker-based measurement. In Kenya, the primary source of population-level biomarker data is the 2015 Kenya STEPwise survey for NCD risk factors (STEPS), which recorded standardised blood pressure measurements and fasting blood glucose in a nationally representative adult sample [@kenyaSTEPS2015]. While the clinical cascade of care in STEPS 2015 has been thoroughly documented [@mohamed2018prevalence; @mohamed2018diabetes], no previous study has bridged the measurement gap between STEPS and KDHS to evaluate how much disease is captured—or omitted—by the self-reported denominators that underpin Kenya's health financing literature.

This study quantifies the detection ratio and underdiagnosis index for hypertension and diabetes in Kenya, benchmarked between STEPS 2015 and KDHS 2022. We evaluate how the choice of denominator alters population-level treatment estimates, document substantial sex divergence in case detection, and assess the implications for health financing monitoring under the Social Health Authority.

# Methods

## Study design and reporting

This investigation is a comparative secondary analysis of two independent, nationally representative cross-sectional surveys: the Kenya STEPS 2015 survey and the Kenya Demographic and Health Survey 2022. The study adheres to the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) reporting guidelines [@vonelm2007strobe]. Because the surveys sampled independent households seven years apart, no individual-level data linkage was conducted; all analyses compare population-level survey-weighted estimates.

## Data sources and variable definitions

**Kenya STEPS 2015.** The 2015 STEPS survey implemented the standard WHO STEPwise approach, capturing behavioural risk factors (Step 1), physical anthropometry and blood pressure (Step 2), and biochemical measurements (Step 3) among adults aged 18–69 years across all 47 counties [@kenyaSTEPS2015]. Blood pressure was measured using validated digital monitors (OMRON HEM-705PC) with three consecutive readings taken at three-minute intervals; following WHO guidelines, the mean of the second and third readings was used for analysis. **Measured hypertension** was defined as mean systolic blood pressure (SBP) $\ge$140 mmHg, mean diastolic blood pressure (DBP) $\ge$90 mmHg, or current self-reported use of prescribed antihypertensive medication. Capillary fasting blood glucose was measured following an overnight fast using point-of-care analyzers (CardioChek PA). **Measured diabetes** was defined as fasting blood glucose $\ge$7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL) or current use of insulin or oral hypoglycaemic agents.

**KDHS 2022.** The 2022 KDHS sampled households nationally, administering individual questionnaires to women aged 15–49 and men aged 15–54 [@kdhs2022]. In KDHS 2022, biological measurements of blood pressure and blood glucose were not collected. Instead, NCD status was ascertained via self-report: respondents were asked whether they had ever been told by a doctor, nurse, or healthcare worker that they had high blood pressure (`sh07`) or diabetes (`sh12`). Current treatment was defined as taking prescribed medication among those reporting a diagnosis (`sh08`, `sh13`). Health insurance coverage was ascertained through the Person Recode file (`sh27`), linked deterministically to individual respondents using cluster, household, and individual line identifiers (`v001/v002/v003` for women and `mv001/mv002/mv003` for men), consistent with established KDHS 2022 architectural rules [@amollo2026st03].

## Denominator architecture in KDHS 2022

A critical methodological feature of KDHS 2022 is the survey questionnaire split. The chronic disease module was administered exclusively in households selected for the Long Questionnaire (`sshort == 0`, encompassing 14,879 women aged 18–49). Women in households administered the Short Questionnaire (`sshort == 1`, n = 15,255) were not eligible for the module and have legitimate missing values (`NaN`). Coding unasked women as non-diagnosed (0)—a common error in secondary analyses—artificially doubles the female denominator and cuts reported prevalence in half. To ensure unbiased population estimates, we restricted the female analytic sample to Long Questionnaire respondents and applied stratum-specific reweighting factors:

$$w_i^* = w_i \times \frac{\sum_{j \in S} w_j^{\text{total}}}{\sum_{k \in S_{\text{long}}} w_k^{\text{long}}}$$

where $S$ denotes the sampling stratum. For men, the individual questionnaire was administered to a one-third subsample of households, and standard male subsample weights (`mv005 / 1e6`) were applied. The pooled adult sample was constructed by concatenating the reweighted female and male files.

## Analytical base and age comparability

KDHS samples women aged 15–49 and men aged 15–54, whereas STEPS samples adults aged 18–69. Because NCD prevalence and health-seeking behaviour rise sharply with age, comparing non-standardised full-survey ranges introduces substantial age-composition bias. To achieve methodological comparability, we established the **overlapping age window of 18–49 years** as the primary analytical base for both surveys. Secondary estimates are presented for the full survey ranges (18–69 in STEPS; 18–49 for women and 18–54 for men in KDHS).

## Awareness definitions

In STEPS 2015, awareness was queried in two stages: whether the respondent had ever been told they had raised blood pressure (`h2a`), and whether this diagnosis occurred within the past 12 months (`h2b`). Previous national cascade analyses adopted the narrower 12-month criterion [@mohamed2018prevalence]. We computed and report awareness under both definitions: **Aware (Ever Told)** and **Aware (12 Months)**. Empirical cross-tabulation confirmed that all participants reporting current medication were also aware; medication adds no uncaptured individuals to awareness.

## Statistical analysis and inference

For each condition, we estimated measured prevalence ($p_{\text{meas}}$) from STEPS and self-reported diagnosis prevalence ($p_{\text{dx}}$) from KDHS. We defined the **detection ratio (DR)** and **underdiagnosis index (UDI)** as:

$$\text{DR} = \frac{p_{\text{dx}}}{p_{\text{meas}}}, \qquad \text{UDI} = \max\left(0, \; 1 - \text{DR}\right)$$

In STEPS, survey weights matched the measurement step (`wstep2` for blood pressure, `wstep3` for glucose). In KDHS, individual weights with questionnaire and subsample adjustments were applied. 

Because the detection ratio combines estimates across two independent, complex survey designs, standard analytical variance formulas cannot capture joint sampling variability. We implemented a **stratified bootstrap** resampling primary sampling units (PSUs) with replacement within survey strata, with 2,000 replications (seed: 20260918). STEPS and KDHS were resampled independently, and the full estimation pipeline was executed within each bootstrap replicate. Confidence intervals (95% CI) were constructed using the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the replicate distribution. Analysis was performed using Python 3.11 with `numpy` and `pandas`.

## Ethical approval

This study is a secondary analysis of publicly available, de-identified survey data. KDHS microdata were accessed under ICF DHS Program authorisation (reference 220623). Kenya STEPS 2015 microdata were accessed under authorized research protocols through the WHO NCD Microdata Repository. The primary surveys received ethical clearance from the Kenya Medical Research Institute (KEMRI) Scientific and Ethics Review Unit and the ICF Institutional Review Board.

# Results

## Measured prevalence versus self-reported diagnosis

Among Kenyan adults aged 18–49 years, measured hypertension prevalence in STEPS 2015 was **19.8% (95% CI 17.5% to 22.5%)**, based on 741 measured cases among 3,500 respondents (Table 1). In contrast, self-reported diagnosis prevalence in KDHS 2022 was **6.6% (95% CI 6.2% to 7.1%)**, based on 1,678 diagnosed cases among 26,487 eligible respondents. Across the full survey age spans, measured prevalence was 24.2% (95% CI 21.8% to 26.8%; n = 1,229/4,443) while self-reported prevalence was 6.8% (95% CI 6.4% to 7.2%; n = 1,770/27,271).

For diabetes, measured prevalence in the 18–49 age window was 1.3% (95% CI 0.9% to 1.7%; n = 60/3,292), compared with a self-reported diagnosis prevalence of 0.9% (95% CI 0.8% to 1.1%; n = 240/26,487). Across the full age range, measured diabetes prevalence reached 2.0% (95% CI 1.4% to 2.6%; n = 119/4,180) compared with 1.0% (95% CI 0.9% to 1.2%; n = 265/27,271) by self-report.

## Detection ratios and the underdiagnosis gap

In the primary age-comparable population (18–49 years), the pooled detection ratio for hypertension was **0.334 (95% CI 0.288 to 0.383)**, corresponding to an underdiagnosis index of **66.6% (95% CI 61.7% to 71.2%)** (Table 3). This demonstrates that self-reported diagnosis omits two out of every three adults living with hypertension. Across the full survey age range, the detection ratio was 0.281 (95% CI 0.250 to 0.315), with an underdiagnosis index of 71.9% (95% CI 68.5% to 75.0%).

For diabetes, the age-comparable detection ratio was 0.754 (95% CI 0.536 to 1.116) and the underdiagnosis index was 24.6% (95% CI 0.0% to 46.4%). Across the full age range, the diabetes detection ratio was 0.521 (95% CI 0.368 to 0.762), corresponding to an underdiagnosis index of 47.9% (95% CI 23.8% to 63.2%).

## Severe gender disparity in case detection

Hypertension detection exhibited marked, statistically significant divergence by sex. Among women aged 18–49, measured hypertension prevalence was 17.5% (95% CI 15.2% to 20.1%; n = 413/2,099) and self-reported diagnosis prevalence was 9.5% (95% CI 8.8% to 10.3%; n = 1,307/14,879), yielding a detection ratio of **0.542 (95% CI 0.459 to 0.638)** and an underdiagnosis index of 45.8% (95% CI 36.2% to 54.1%).

Among men aged 18–49, measured prevalence was higher at 22.2% (95% CI 19.0% to 25.8%; n = 328/1,401), but self-reported diagnosis was merely 3.3% (95% CI 2.9% to 3.8%; n = 371/11,608). Consequently, the detection ratio in men dropped to **0.151 (95% CI 0.123 to 0.185)**, with an underdiagnosis index of **84.9% (95% CI 81.5% to 87.7%)**. Working-age Kenyan men with hypertension face an underdiagnosis rate nearly double that of women: fewer than one in six hypertensive men have been identified by the health system.

## Population-level consequences of the hidden denominator

Translating these parameters to the entire population reveals the scale of unaddressed chronic disease. Among all Kenyan adults aged 18–49, **16.2% (95% CI 14.3% to 18.4%)** lived with hypertension of which they were completely unaware, and **19.4% (95% CI 17.0% to 22.1%)** lived with uncontrolled hypertension (Table 1). The unaware burden was disproportionately male: 20.0% (95% CI 17.1% to 23.1%) of men versus 12.6% (95% CI 10.7% to 14.6%) of women carried undiagnosed hypertension.

When evaluated within the self-report denominator alone, 32.1% (95% CI 29.0% to 35.2%) of diagnosed adults in KDHS 2022 reported taking antihypertensive medication, and 45.6% (95% CI 42.3% to 48.8%) were covered by health insurance. However, because self-report captures only 6.6% of the adult population, scaling medication use to the total population demonstrates that treatment reaches only **2.1% (95% CI 1.9% to 2.4%)** of adults aged 18–49 (3.1% among women, 1.1% among men). The 97.9% of the population not receiving treatment comprises both diagnosed individuals not on medication and the vast undiagnosed majority.

## Reconciling awareness definitions in the STEPS cascade

In STEPS 2015, awareness among adults aged 18–49 with measured hypertension was 18.1% (95% CI 13.9% to 22.6%) under the "ever told" definition, but fell to 12.2% (95% CI 8.5% to 16.8%) under the 12-month definition (Table 2). Across the full survey range (18–69 years), awareness was 23.7% (95% CI 20.0% to 27.7%) under "ever told" and 16.0% (95% CI 12.6% to 20.2%) under the 12-month criterion. The 16.0% estimate aligns closely with the 15.6% (95% CI 12.4% to 18.9%) age-standardised figure reported by Mohamed et al. [@mohamed2018prevalence]. 

Treatment conditional on awareness differed substantially between definitions: at ages 18–49, treatment was 29.5% (95% CI 19.4% to 38.9%) among those ever told, but 43.7% (95% CI 32.0% to 53.3%) among those told within 12 months, reflecting recent clinical engagement. Population control among all individuals with measured hypertension was 2.2% (95% CI 0.6% to 4.9%) at ages 18–49 and 2.7% (95% CI 1.3% to 4.6%) across the full age span.

# Discussion

## Principal findings

This study provides the first direct empirical benchmarking of Kenya's self-reported NCD survey data against population biomarker measurements. Our findings indicate that self-reported diagnosis captures only one in three Kenyan adults aged 18–49 living with hypertension (detection ratio 0.334, 95% CI 0.288 to 0.383), leaving two-thirds (66.6%) of the disease burden completely unobserved in self-report surveys. 

Crucially, our analysis uncovers an alarming gender gap in case detection. While women have a detection ratio of 0.542 (more than half diagnosed), men exhibit a detection ratio of only 0.151, meaning that nearly 85% of working-age Kenyan men with hypertension are undiagnosed. At the population level, 16.2% of all adults—and 20.0% of men—carry undiagnosed hypertension. Consequently, when national surveys report treatment rates among diagnosed individuals (32.1%), this translates to active treatment reaching a meager 2.1% of the adult population.

## Methodological implications for health financing research

These findings fundamentally alter how DHS-based health financing and health systems analyses must be interpreted [@amollo2026st03; @oyando2022inequality]. Household surveys like KDHS are indispensable for tracking equity, financial hardship, and insurance coverage across demographic strata. However, when health financing evaluations restrict their sample to respondents with self-reported diagnoses, they do not describe the financing needs of the population with disease. Rather, they describe a selected minority who have successfully interacted with the health system, obtained clinical screening, and retained knowledge of their diagnostic status.

The remaining two-thirds of the hypertensive population—and five-sixths of hypertensive men—have an effective treatment gap of 100%, because an unrecognised condition cannot be treated. Health financing studies that report high out-of-pocket costs or low insurance coverage among diagnosed individuals describe the financial friction of *staying in care*, but they remain entirely blind to the financial barriers to *entering care* (e.g., transport costs, lost wages, and diagnostic fees for asymptomatic screening). Treating self-reported cases as the total denominator risks misdirecting health financing reforms toward subsidising drugs for the few while ignoring the system investments needed to detect the many.

## Structural drivers of the male detection deficit

The striking sex disparity in detection (54.2% in women vs 15.1% in men) reflects structural features of Kenya's primary healthcare architecture. Working-age women have multiple routine institutional touchpoints with primary healthcare facilities through reproductive, maternal, newborn, and child health (RMNCH) services [@kdhs2022]. Routine antenatal care (ANC) protocols mandate blood pressure screening at every visit to detect pre-eclampsia and gestational hypertension, providing young women with repeated opportunistic screening. 

In contrast, working-age men have virtually no structural contact with primary health facilities prior to the onset of severe, symptomatic illness or acute cardiovascular complications. Facility-based healthcare in Kenya remains largely reactive rather than proactive. Men frequently cite direct out-of-pocket consultation fees, long waiting times, facility operating hours that conflict with informal employment, and gendered social norms around illness vulnerability as formidable barriers to seeking care [@amollo2026kisumu]. Without institutionalised opportunistic screening tailored to male routines, men remain undetected until hypertensive crisis, stroke, or heart failure occurs.

## Implications for Social Health Authority (SHA) monitoring

These findings have direct implications for Kenya's ongoing health financing overhaul under the Social Health Authority [@nungo2024]. If SHA monitoring and evaluation frameworks track universal health coverage solely through claims data or household self-report surveys, the health system risks tracking an illusion of progress. A program could dramatically increase insurance coverage and medication adherence among diagnosed patients, yet have virtually no impact on population-level cardiovascular mortality if 85% of hypertensive men remain undetected.

To achieve genuine UHC, SHA policy must address two structural imperatives:
1. **Case detection must be prioritised as a core financing benefit.** The Primary Healthcare Fund under SHA must explicitly finance community-based, workplace, and non-facility screening initiatives. Primary Care Networks (PCNs) should deploy Community Health Promoters (CHPs) equipped with validated digital blood pressure monitors to actively screen men at gathering sites, markets, transport hubs, and agricultural centers.
2. **Periodic biomarker surveillance is mandatory.** Household self-report cannot substitute for physical measurement. Kenya's only national biomarker survey (STEPS) was conducted in 2015—over a decade ago. Establishing regular biomarker monitoring (either via periodic STEPS surveys or integrating physical measurement modules into future DHS rounds) is not an academic luxury; it is a foundational prerequisite for evaluating whether SHA financing is reaching the populations with true biological need.

## Strengths and limitations

Key strengths of this study include the use of two nationally representative surveys, rigorous design-based survey weighting, deterministic household questionnaire adjustment in KDHS 2022, dual-cascade reconciliation with published literature [@mohamed2018prevalence], and fully propagated stratified PSU bootstrap inference across both independent sampling frames.

Several limitations must be acknowledged. First, the two surveys were conducted seven years apart (2015 and 2022). Our detection ratio benchmarks two measurement systems across time; it cannot distinguish between static underdiagnosis and potential improvements in healthcare access between 2015 and 2022. If diagnostic screening improved over the period, the true contemporaneous detection ratio would be somewhat higher, and underdiagnosis lower, than estimated here. Nonetheless, the magnitude of the gap (66.6% overall and 84.9% in men) is far too large to be explained by seven-year secular trends alone. Second, age structures do not perfectly align across surveys; however, restricting the primary analysis to ages 18–49 resolved this for the working-age population. Third, biomarker hypertension in STEPS was determined during a single survey visit (mean of two readings), which may overestimate sustained hypertension due to white-coat effects, whereas clinical diagnosis requires repeated visits. Finally, measured diabetes case counts were small (60 cases in the 18–49 group), resulting in wide bootstrap intervals; diabetes detection estimates should be regarded as exploratory.

# Conclusions

Self-reported diagnosis omits two out of every three Kenyan adults living with hypertension, and over 80% of hypertensive men. Health financing analyses based on self-reported survey data do not measure population-level treatment gaps; they document service delivery among a detected minority. As Kenya rolls out the Social Health Authority, financing mechanisms must actively fund proactive, community-based case detection targeting men, and national monitoring systems must incorporate periodic biomarker surveillance to evaluate true population health impact.
